sections.title: Chunking Long Documents for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
sections.content: A. Example and B. Sample Example Institute of Technology

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Retrieval-augmented generation answers questions from a collection of documents, but long documents must first be split into passages. We compare fixed-size word windows with section-aware chunking on a set of synthetic papers and find that section-aware chunks keep related sentences together, which improves answer grounding.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content:
Large language models answer questions fluently, yet they cannot cite sources they have never seen. Retrieval-augmented generation addresses this by searching a document collection and passing the most relevant passages to the model. The quality of those passages depends on how the documents were split.
This paper studies that split. We describe a hybrid strategy that keeps medium-sized sections whole, merges very short sections with their neighbours, and divides very long sections into overlapping windows.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Earlier systems used fixed windows of a few hundred words with a small overlap between consecutive windows. Other work splits on sentence boundaries or uses the layout of the source document to find headings.

sections.title: 3 Method
sections.content: Each document is first converted into a sequence of text items, each labelled as a title, a section header or ordinary text. Section headers start new sections; all other text is appended to the current section.

sections.title: 3.1 Window Size
sections.content: Sections longer than eight hundred words are split into windows of six hundred words that overlap by one hundred words. Every window repeats the paper title and abstract so that it can be understood on its own.

sections.title: 4 Experiments
sections.content:
We built two hundred synthetic papers and asked one question per paper. Section-aware chunks answered more questions correctly than fixed windows, and the answers cited the right section more often.
The gains were largest for papers with many short sections, where fixed windows mixed unrelated topics.

sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: Splitting documents along their own structure is a simple change that makes retrieved passages more coherent. Future work will look at tables and figures, which this study ignored.

sections.title: References
sections.content:
